utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. The witness should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning. Please sit down. I would like to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies, and Mr. Thayer has some more for questions for you. Mr. Thayer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you and Your Honours. Good morning, General Tolimir, Mr. Gajic. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Blaszczyk.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to pick up where we left off yesterday and that was concerning a radio telephone conversation between Colonel Savcic and Major Malinic on the 13th of July, 1995, which Colonel Savcic testified about in the Popovic case and during which he recalled that General Tolimir was standing right next to Colonel Savcic during that conversation. You recall that just yesterday when we left off, Mr. Blaszczyk?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 1D118 on e-court, please. That's Colonel Savcic's testimony in the Popovic case. And if we could go to page 22, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. As we can see at transcript page 15252 in the Popovic case and then again, just for the record, a couple of pages later at 15254, line 19, Colonel Savcic testified that the conversation we were speaking about yesterday was actually the second conversation which he had with Major Malinic that day, 13 July. And in the first conversation - and again for the record this is at transcript 15249 of the Popovic testimony - in that first conversation sometime in the early morning hours Colonel Savcic testified that Major Malinic described only three Muslims surrendering; but by the second conversation, the one he said General Tolimir was present for, Major Malinic told Colonel Savcic that the situation had become much more complex and that there were so many Muslims surrendering that he didn't have enough soldiers to guard them. Do you recall the gist of that testimony by Colonel Savcic in the Popovic case, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just remind us again, what was Major Malinic's position in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Malinic was the commander of the military battalion of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 26 in e-court, please; this is page 15256 in the transcript in Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say "military battalion of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment," do you mean to say the military police battalion, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. It's military police battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when we look at page 26 here in e-court we can see that Colonel Savcic is testifying about this change in situation by the increase of the prisoners and that it was this changed circumstance that General Tolimir was present for during the discussion. This was the nature of the discussion that General Tolimir was present for. Now, yesterday at transcript page 3698 at line 9, General Tolimir quoted the following to you from Colonel Savcic's Popovic testimony. And he quoted from page 15263.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 33 in e-court, we'll just pop that up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He quoted a lengthy passage and then -- and this is all referring to P125, the document that we've been spending so much time on. And I'll just refer to that as the Borike memo, the memo that Danko Gojkovic testified about that refers to the thousand prisoners at Kasaba. And we see here at line 3 - and this is the last line that General Tolimir quoted to you yesterday - he quoted General Savcic here. "All I can say is that this document was never received by the military police commander ..." Again, that's a reference to P125. And General Tolimir ended the quote there. Now, I don't think there's any dispute that this military police commander that this refers to here is Major Malinic. And I'm sure that if General Tolimir disagrees he'll let us know. Now, let's look at some more of General Savcic's testimony which General Tolimir didn't quote to you yesterday, and let's look at the very next line, line 9, where General Savcic, if there were any doubt, says: I have -- "I base that on the statement by Major Malinic." So in that portion that General Tolimir quoted to you, "all I can say is that this document was never received by the military police commander ..." it may seem obvious, sir, but is that referring to Major Malinic allegedly never receiving the document?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we go down to line 12, and this is another portion that General Tolimir didn't quote to you yesterday, we see that Colonel Savcic is basing his claim that Major Malinic allegedly never received the telegram, not on any conversation he had with Major Malinic in July of 1995 or at any time in 1995, but on a single conversation he had with Malinic sometime after General Savcic's OTP interview. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you know off the top of your head when in 2005 General Savcic was interviewed by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I remember the year, it was 2005, but I don't remember the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you can take my word for it that it was in October 2005, and if General Tolimir disagrees, I'm sure he'll let us know about that as well. Now, do you recall yesterday when General Tolimir quoted to you from General Savcic's testimony and I objected that he was being selective in his quotations. Do you remember that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact at transcript page 3700 yesterday General Tolimir claimed, and I quote: "I haven't read anything about Major Malinic ..." Do you remember him saying that to the Trial Chamber yesterday?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, despite not quoting any of these portions to you, General Tolimir repeated yesterday - and this is at transcript page 3703, line 9, that's three pages after claiming that he didn't read anything about Major Malinic - General Tolimir repeated, and I quote: "Does Savcic claim in his testimony that the commander of the military police never received this document?" Do you remember that from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And you answered at line 12 that, and I quote: "I think he says also that he never discussed the contents of this document or whatever, the order, you know, with the commander of the military battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment, if I correctly remember the transcript."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now can we go to the next page in e-court, please, and this is transcript page 15264 of Colonel Savcic's Popovic testimony, page 34 in e-court. And this was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Continue, and then Mr. Tolimir before the witness answers. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I welcome everybody present and may God protect you and may God's will be done. May the outcome be as God wishes and not as I wish. If Mr. Thayer is quoting me, what I said for the transcript, then he should quote me saying that the commander of the battalion, without mentioning his name, never received this telegram or acted upon it which is very important. He didn't act upon the telegram because he never received it. But Mr. Thayer doesn't want to say so, doesn't want to say how it was in the transcript. He is putting it totally differently and he is reproducing my words his own way. Please consider this, because what I said for the transcript yesterday should be reproduced fairly and accurately. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think even the briefest reading of the transcript will show that I am simply quoting verbatim what General Tolimir told this Trial Chamber yesterday. And if he's got any cites to the record to the contrary, then I'm sure he will let us know. If I may continue with my examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just to avoid any misunderstanding, can you again give us the -- I think you did it already. But where is the reference from what Mr. Tolimir was saying yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There are a couple of references, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Only the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The first one was at 3700, where he claimed that "I haven't read anything about Major Malinic," that was at transcript page 3700. Then he repeated again at 3703, line 9: "Does Savcic claim in his testimony that the commander of the military police never received this document?" And I've already cited to the witness the portion that General Tolimir claims I did not do, which was his selective reading of General Savcic's testimony yesterday which ended with the question about -- or the allegation that Major Malinic never received this order. I went through all that with the witness about five minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir -- just a moment. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that I was misquoted by the Prosecutor because what had been interpreted to me is something that I said at the end. The sentence was that the commander of the battalion never received the telegram or act upon it which is very important because these were important activities. And now this element of acting upon it is now being left out. Look at what I said yesterday when I finished reading out what my advisor, what my consultant, translated to me, especially the last sentence. That must be borne in mind because acting is rather different from receiving something. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we have your position now on the record. This is quite clear. And Mr. Thayer should continue his re-examination. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at page 15264, I want to focus on a portion I'd wanted to show you yesterday, and that's when General Tolimir claimed that Mr. Gajic hadn't given it to him because he doesn't read English. Now -- actually, by the way, Mr. Blaszczyk, are you aware that the OTP has furnished General Tolimir with the audio recordings of the Popovic testimony in his own language?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at line 13 on this page, Mr. Vanderpuye asked Colonel Savcic if when he spoke with Major Malinic about the telegram, did he discuss the specifics of it with Major Malinic in that single conversation in 2005. And if we look at Colonel Savcic's response at line 16, he says: "No. To be honest, I didn't. The document was not available to me. I didn't have it on me. Mr. McCloskey had shown it to me in Banja Luka, and we had discussed this document. So I did not go into the contents of the document. I just inquired about the existence of the document. I asked him whether he remembered that he received a telegram from me on the 13th of July. Since he said that he didn't, I really didn't go into the details of the contents of the document. I just told him that it referred to the treatment of prisoners of war. I really did not try to retain the contents, bullet point by bullet point, so I could not discuss the details with anybody." Sir, is that the testimony you were referring to yesterday when you said "if I correctly remember the transcript"? Is that the testimony you were thinking about?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to spend a little bit more time talking about how you, as an investigator, authenticated this document, P125. We looked at three intercepts yesterday. And to save time I didn't put up the print-outs, but we've got all morning, so I'm not going to use that as an invitation to waste time but I want to show the print-outs now that we have the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we see P410B, please. And this is under seal, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Looking at the original B/C/S on the left-hand screen, sir, do you see a date of this intercept report?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is on the left-hand corner. There is the date of the report, the date 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what is the time on the first intercept that you see reported on there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yesterday I objected that in the re-examination questions were being put about which the witness hasn't been asked either in the direct examination or in the cross-examination. This witness has been brought here to tender the Drina Corps documents through him, but now the Prosecutor is now interpreting documents of the Federation through this witness. He is trying to tender some conversations from transcripts made at a time after the document was made. Can this be right if a conversation took place -- we saw two conversations yesterday, one at 1405, one at 1402. Can that be a foundation for the contents of a telegram? We're talking about the authenticity of a document. I don't know whether Mr. Thayer is saying that Savcic was at Borike and whether I was invited there to hear the conversation. Is that what he's trying to put to you? If so, then he must get Savcic here and not this witness who isn't an expert for transcripts. I haven't discussed the contents of any document with him, only the authenticity. I didn't want to embarrass him. In the first cross-examination he said that he found the document as it was in the archives of the Drina Corps; but yesterday he said that he received it from Colonel Acimovic. Yesterday he said that since they left to Gornji Milanovac, the documents were never in the possession of its users again, but that they went to the MUP and from the MUP to the Ministry of Defence and from there to Zagreb, and that the documents were under the control of the Tribunal. I don't want to embarrass anybody. I didn't want to point that out because I didn't mind. I didn't want to embarrass the witness. But please consider that this re-examination should not try to turn this witness into something else. Because he seems to be becoming an expert for all sorts of things, maybe even the air force. I only discussed the authenticity of the documents, about the fact that Savcic was not at the command post at Borike. And if the Prosecutor's arguing the contrary, then he must show documents to support his claims. The more so since this is a witness who worked for the Prosecution. And now it is easy to construe things. How does he know about transcripts and conversations now? I only spoke about the Drina Corps with him, the documents of that corps. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We -- the Chamber understood your point. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, General Tolimir well knows the importance of authenticating the Drina Corps collection documents to this case, and he clearly well knows the critical importance of P125 to establishing his guilt in this case. Had he not known, he wouldn't have spent so much time challenging the authenticity of that document by talking about teleprinters, talking about Danko Gojkovic's testimony, trotting out Colonel Savcic's testimony to you, all in an effort, knowingly and well planned and as is his right and as we expected, to challenge the Prosecution's evidence and the authenticity of its documents, in particular the Borike memo. Now, in terms of the immediate issue, this document, yesterday when we reviewed those intercepts General Tolimir specifically objected that there was no date on them. And what I am doing now is simply going through what we can all see, which is the dates. I plan to just go through these two intercepts with the notebooks so that the Trial Chamber can see the dates, in specific response to General Tolimir's objection that he didn't see any date on the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Thayer, the view -- my view, the Prosecution's now challenging your content of the cross-examination. This is the right of a party during re-examination, but it is up to the Chamber to give weight to the content. At the moment we understand the Prosecution as going through evidence related to P125. And we will see what is it about, and I think Mr. Thayer should carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you just note for the record what the time is on this first intercept.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 1300 hours and 55 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would kindly ask the Prosecutor, here in this cross-examination, not to speak about the intentions of the Defence and not to interpret them while he's questioning the witness. He can do that for the Trial Chamber or at a -- with joint agreement of the parties, that's one thing. The second thing is he says Tolimir is guilty; you can see that from this document. He has to specify the type of guilt. This is a document that was created five minutes before the one at Borike. This is a document that Tolimir did not take part in the drafting of, does not know about it -- did not know about it until now. So could he please be a bit more specific about the types of charges here. I would like to be protected from some kind of arbitrary formulations that are being stated here, and this witness is not really competent to discuss these particular matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, to avoid any misunderstanding, Mr. Thayer, in my view, didn't say that you are guilty. It has something to do with the question if guilt can be established during this trial, and this is quite different. And therefore I think you must not be -- have any concern about the protection of your rights. You have rights pursuant to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal and you used quite a lot of time during cross-examination - this is your right - and this is not in any way challenged by the Prosecution. Now the Prosecution is challenging the content of your cross-examination; this is the right of the Prosecution during re-examination. I think your position is very clear. Now we would like to know what is the position of the Prosecution during the continuation of the re-examination. Mr. Thayer, please continue --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Tolimir, it's not the best way just to continue this debate, this discussion, about these topics. Your position is very clear, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, that is your decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we ...

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is it okay to continue, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. May we go forward two pages in the original and stay where we are on the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what the time is on the intercept that's on the left, sir.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell -- well, I'll just leave it there. Okay. So we've got an intercept, 1400 hours. This is the one that we looked at yesterday on the right; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's do the same exercise with P411.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that's 411B, please, the print-out. And this is also under seal. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on the left do you see the original intercept report, sir; and if you do, can you tell us what the date is?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the date of this report is 13th July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us what the time is on the first intercept.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time from the first intercept is 1300 hours, 55 minutes, five minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And is this, in fact, the same print-out that we just looked at a second ago which contains a number of intercepts?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So let's go to three more pages in the original and stay on the English translation -- I'm sorry, one page back in the original. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do we see the intercept at 1400 hours?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is that the one you just identified with the last exhibit?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could scroll down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see an intercept at 1405?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And does this intercept correspond to the one we saw yesterday in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we saw this intercept yesterday. We discussed this intercept yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to talk a little bit about the third intercept that we saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter number 765 on the screen, and this is the notebook of the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You remember this notebook entry from yesterday, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the Trial Chamber has heard testimony that there were three units working as intercept operators at one of the locations, the northern one. Those units were the 2nd Corps, the MUP, and the 21st Division. Are you familiar with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I think we can probably all recite in our sleep the testimony that we heard over and over again from the ABiH 2nd Corps intercept operators who testified about writing all their intercepts in the notebooks but not writing the dates in the notebooks because they knew that the typist cryptographer was going to enter the date in the notebook. Are you familiar with all that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, yesterday the Trial Chamber heard, I believe, from the first 21st Division intercept operator witness, and if my memory serves, he said that in their notebooks, the 21st Division operators noted the date in the notebook every day. Are you familiar with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at the notebook that this notebook on the screen came out of, and I've got the original here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we may have 65 ter 1670 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have an objection because this was also not a part of the examination-in-chief or the cross-examination, and now we're talking about this in the redirect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, General Tolimir objected yesterday that he didn't see any dates connected with the intercepts, and what I am doing now is showing the witness a notebook in which I think that question will be clearly answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. Thayer asked the witness if he recalled the conversation. He said "I do," as if he were the one who intercepted it. So it's not the date and the time; we're talking about the contents here. That is the essence of my objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question was: "Are you familiar with all that testimony, sir?" And the answer is: "Yes, I do." This is page 16, line 3 and 4. This is quite different from what you stated just now. Please carry on, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President. We're having a little bit of an e-court glitch at the moment. I think we'll -- what we can do is do this the old-fashioned way and use the ELMO as a backup here because we've got the wrong exhibit on e-court, but we've got the original here for everybody to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Court Usher will assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We need to zoom out a little bit, if we could, so we catch the cover. Okay. For the record, we have a notebook with the ERN 0078-1141 on the cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is the witness in a position to have it on the screen as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't have it on the screen, but I have the original here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you'd -- you might have to twist around a little bit, Mr. Blaszczyk, but if you can work with the original.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There are two dates towards the top of the notebook here. They're kind of hard to see on the ELMO. Can you read out what those dates there, and if there are words next to them that you can read and interpret for us, please do; if you can't, then just give us the dates that you see at the top of the notebook.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I use the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yeah, just pick up the original and feel free to just read the ...

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two dates. The first date is when the book was opened, in fact; it's 29 June 1995. And the date when "zatvoren," which means "closed," the book was closed, 23 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could open up that notebook, please, and go to the first page with writing on it. Okay. And for the record this is ERN 0078-1143. Okay. Do we see any date on this page, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see a date here. I see a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could flip a couple pages, and if you want to just do it slowly, we'll go to the next page, 1143 to 1144, 1145, if you can slide it over so we can just see 1144 first. Perfect. Thank you. We don't see any dates there. 1145. Now if we can look at 1146, do you see any dates there? 1147. Next page, 1148. And then how about the next page, 1149.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This page is visible date, 30 June 1995, Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If you could scoot the book over just a little bit so we can see the ERN on that page. Okay. So you said the cover of the book had a date of 29 June 1995, when you said the book was opened, and now here we have the first date of 30 June 1995. Now, can you flip to the page that we saw a few minutes ago on the screen in the notebook, and that's the ERN 0078-1236. Can you just find that page, sir. Okay. And is this the intercept notebook page that we saw a few minutes ago with the time of 1602 hours, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Is there a date on this page?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see any date here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Then let's work backwards and see if we can find a date for this notebook. Can you turn back to 1235. Okay. Do you see a date there, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, in the previous page is date 13 July 1995, first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is there a time for that first intercept there?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the time is 0800 hours and 08, eight minutes past 8.00, if I see correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We're done with this exhibit. Mr. President, I thought that we had a 65 ter number which is what we tried to put up on the screen, but it turns out that's connected to apparently a different notebook. So I'm not sure if we have a 65 ter number for this entire notebook. We certainly had a 65 ter number for the intercept that came out of it. We'll explore that with you and we may have to come back and just provide a 65 ter number and apply to add that to the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think in this case we have to deal with a lot of problems with numbers and MFI'd documents, and so on. But please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We're done with that, Mr. Blaszczyk. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the document at 1602, can that be the basis to prove the authenticity of the document? Well, Mr. Thayer can say whether that can be used for the document which was created at 1406, and was there a command post there, was General Savcic there, was Tolimir there, was he a participant in one of those conversations? Can we clarify this with the witness because it is also within the context of the testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General Tolimir well knows what the context of this testimony is and the purpose for which these intercepts are being shown. And I'm going to turn directly now to P125, the Borike memo to continue showing how this document was authenticated by Mr. Blaszczyk in the investigation, which lay at the heart of General Tolimir's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First, is it possible to show the original notebook to the accused and to the Chamber, please. Secondly, Mr. Tolimir, the Chamber is at this stage not in a position to say anything about authenticity of the document. We just listen and we review all the evidence, the documentary evidence, and the testimony of witnesses at a later stage. There's no comment on that at the moment. We just receive evidence. Wait a moment, please, Mr. Thayer. We would like to have a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May this document be given to the accused and Mr. Gajic. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. I don't want to look at this document. I'm not the participant in the document. I'm talking about the document 525 that we can see on the screen. I contested its authenticity. There's a possibility that it just found its way there or that somebody planted it there because there is nothing else other than the copy of this document. This is what I would like to say about the document with the number 525. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. But it is P125, what we have on the screen now, not 525.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for correcting me. Yes, this is P125. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's take a look at the -- towards the top of this Borike document. We see that it's headed "Procedure for treatment of prisoners of war," and I think we've been through this before, but it never hurts to repeat. Can you tell us who the actual officers are by name that are referred to in the recipient portion where it says "to." And let's just start first with the commander of the VRS Main Staff. July 1995, who's that?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska army in July 1995 was General Mladic, Ratko Mladic. Assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs of the Main Staff of VRS was General Gvero. And commander of the military police battalion of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment was Major Malinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then we see that this is captioned as an "order." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we spent some time looking at evidence concerning these thousand -- over a thousand Muslim soldiers that are referred to in the first line of this document. That's why we went through all the intercepts and everything else thus far. Let's look at where it says: "Assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs of the VRS Main Staff proposes the following measures ..." Let's look at proposed measure number 1. Do you see where it says that: "Prohibit access to unauthorised individuals, filming and photographing of prisoners."

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Based on your investigation, Mr. Blaszczyk, what organs within the VRS were responsible for guarding and escorting prisoners?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was security organ of VRS, military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in July 1995 who was the chief of security within the VRS?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of security and intelligence was General Tolimir, but chief of security was Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object again because all the combat documents, directives, orders, are being misrepresented deliberate -- misrepresented here. And what is the idea is to be imputing this assignment to somebody else. I don't know if this witness is an expert, and then if he is an expert in these matters, he can read the document and then explain what the term "to be responsible for prisoners" means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the question was clear and it was understood by the witness and we have his answer, and I would like to move to the second line if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you raised an objection, but in fact I don't understand that. What is the essence of your objection? I would like to know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The gist of my objection is that the -- Mr. Thayer has put a suggestive -- a leading question to the witness, and he's saying this is put forward by Tolimir. But if the investigator studied his matter well, he will know that the assistant for logistics would be the one who is responsible for the prisoners and not the chief of intelligence. So we're having an erroneous answer here and erroneous conclusions are being drawn on the basis of this document. So I would like the -- both conclusions and everything else to rely strictly on what is said in the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer read out precisely what is written in the document, and I haven't heard that he has said and put to the witness that Mr. Tolimir was responsible for logistics. I haven't heard that. Please carry on, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at - thank you, Mr. President - proposed measure number 2, where it says: "Prohibit traffic for all United Nations vehicles ..." and then it lays out a route. Based on your investigations, sir, what organs within the VRS were responsible for regulating traffic and setting up check-points?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was military police of VRS under the command of security branch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The security department never had police in its ranks nor was it superior to the police. This is a plot of the Prosecution to put responsibility on Tolimir because the security --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- department is not responsible for the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is not a correct objection. We receive answers from the witness and it is up to the Chamber at the end, and you may then put your case to the Chamber, if we can believe it what the witness says or not. He -- this witness is very clearly not an eye-witness. He was not present when the war was going on. He is testifying about the results and the way of his investigation. That's a big difference. And it's up to the Chamber and the parties at the end of the trial to find a solution. It's not appropriate now to comment every answer of the witness. Mr. Thayer, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at proposed measure number 3 where it says that the: "Commander of the military police battalion shall take measures to remove war prisoners from the main Milici-Zvornik road, place them somewhere indoors or in an area protected from observation from the ground or air." Now, we see that there's a reference to observation from the ground or air. Is there any reference in this Borike memo to -- proposal to protection from bombing?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did the Muslims, the Muslim army, have any combat aircraft based on your investigation that you know of in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about it. I'm not aware about such forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How about NATO? Did NATO have combat aircraft available in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course NATO had combat planes available.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, focusing on this proposal here to place the prisoners out of sight from being seen both -- not just from the air in a helicopter or airplane but also from people on the ground, can you tell the Trial Chamber based on your investigation where the prisoners who were captured and gathered at Nova Kasaba were taken on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the prisoners who were captured and kept at the beginning in Nova Kasaba soccer field were taken to Bratunac in buses and trucks and were kept at the school in Bratunac and also in the hangar behind the school. We call this school Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about the prisoners who were captured and collected and gathered at the Sandici meadow on the 13th of July, where were they taken, Mr. Blaszczyk?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who were guarded -- the Muslim prisoners who were guarded at Sandici meadow were taken also to Kravica warehouse. This is place located from Sandici about 900 metres, 1 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, how about the prisoners who, as you just testified, had been held in Bratunac at the Vuk Karadzic school and in buses around the town of Bratunac, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After -- shortly after that, people were transported to the Zvornik area, also to the -- mostly to the schools in the Zvornik area. It was school Orahovac, Petkovci, Rocevic, Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, did your investigation reveal any evidence that after the 13th of July in the afternoon, when Danko Gojkovic typed this document into the teleprinter and sent it out, that any large groups of prisoners were left outside in the open?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the process of taking out prisoners from the open air was still pending at that time. At 1400 hours the people were taken to Kravica warehouse and Sandici meadow and then from soccer field in Nova Kasaba to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So my question is: After this Borike memo was sent out in the afternoon, and we see on the original 1510 hours, after that memo went out, this Borike proposal and order, did your investigation reveal any evidence that groups of Muslim prisoners were left out in the open?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Most of the people were sent to, as I said, to Bratunac in the houses -- I mean the school in Bratunac, and they were kept in the buses in Kravica; small group also in the junction in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based on your investigation, sir, approximately when did the first large-scale mass executions of the prisoners that had been placed out of sight in those various structures begin?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first mass executions in large scale started in Kravica warehouse, and this was on the 13th of July, 1995, in afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, are you familiar with what Colonel Savcic said in his OTP interview and his Popovic testimony about what this order to keep the prisoners out of sight meant?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think during his testimony he referred something to the possible -- I don't remember, but of course it was in his explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember him saying, among other things, that he was concerned that NATO might --

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- bomb large groups of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was his words and it was -- for me this is unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember him saying in the Popovic case that he thought it might have something to do with the Geneva Conventions banning prisoners from being exposed to public viewing by average people, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at line 4, which is proposed measure number 4. "Once the commander of the military police battalion receives this order, he shall contact General Miletic and receive from him additional orders and verify if the proposal has been approved by the commander of the VRS Main Staff." Who or -- who -- I'm sorry. I'm sounding like an owl. What was General Miletic's position in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July of 1995 General Miletic was the assistant commander for operation -- I mean assistant commander of the Main Staff of VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say he was in the operations field, was he chief of operations and training, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's fair to say. This is his full title.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So he's not actually an assistant commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, not assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to make the record clear about that. Now, did your investigation and your work with the Drina Corps collection documents ever reveal any orders from anyone adopting any of these proposals?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a lot of orders, but I don't know what you mean exactly. Which order?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 2100, please. And this will be the -- I think the last document we'll look at today.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, I just want to give you a minute to look at this document, re-familiarise yourself with it.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I remember this document. I think it was seized also in the collection of -- for sure it was a Drina Corps collection document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 2 of this order and we'll see who it's from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In the English, that is. Okay. Now, can we go back to page 1 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we can see, if we're looking at the original version of this order that it's type-signed, as we refer to it, by whom, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Glavni Stab, Vojska Republika Srpska, this is Main Staff of Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we just look down at the very bottom.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we see the name of General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. A little bit of typo problem there with the teleprinter; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I don't think there's any dispute that this order is emanating -- originating from General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We see two initials or two letters, S. R., after General Mladic's name there if we're looking at bottom of the original. What does "S. R." stand for in your experience in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We would like to have the end of the document in English as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did remember, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try to help you. Have you ever heard that referred to as "in his own hand" or "by own hand"?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Yes, but I don't know the words, the B/C/S words of this expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll, I'm sure, hear more about that with other witnesses. But does that indicate that General Mladic in the original order personally signed and was present to sign the order? Is that what the gist of that initial is, sir, those initials, S. R.?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it means that it was done by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have page 1 of the English back on e-court, please. And if we could scroll up a little bit in the B/C/S -- actually, in both versions, sorry. Thank you. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with the Usher's assistance I'd ask to hand up to you the original of this from out of the Drina Corps collection. And if we can hand it up to the Chamber and to General Tolimir, and I'll ask you a question on it. And I would just draw your attention to the upper right-hand corner of the document. Do you see a signature?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this signature. This is Danko Gojkovic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is that signature in original ink, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And there's some writing and some numbers next to this signature. What does that say? Can you tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in the top of -- above the signature there is the date, 13 July 1995. And word in B/C/S, in Cyrillic, "Primljeno" 2250 minutes. "Primljeno," it means "received." And two letters below "-a/a." This is sent to -- for archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And confirming that this document was received by the Rogatica Brigade below it's very visible right now, in the original, of course, the stamp of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could just scroll down in the original so we can have an idea of what you're talking about there. Okay. Are you referring to the stamp that's in the middle at the very bottom of the page, sir, where it says "komanda"?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am referring to this stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In translation there is not -- not mentioned Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade but -- 1st Light Infantry Brigade, but this is Podrinje -- well known as Rogatica Brigade, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So the illegible word in the translation you can read in the original, and what is that word?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is "Podrinjska." It means Podrinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And what brigade was Danko Gojkovic a teleprinter operator in?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As was said here many times, he was a member of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, so-called Rogatica Brigade member.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now I have to ask you not to overlap. You are speaking in the same language and it is very difficult for the recorder to follow your conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My apologies as well, Mr. President. Okay, if we could ask the Usher to pass that up, please. Thank you, Mr. Usher. Now, if we go back to page 1 of the translation and scroll up a little bit in the original, please. All the way. There we go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now we can -- if we look at the upper left-hand corner of this document, we can see that this order emanates from the Main Staff of the VRS, and there's the strictly confidential number that you spoke about yesterday. And we see the -- we refer to them as ordinals 03/4. Based on your experience, do you know whether those ordinals denote any particular part of the VRS Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we can see that this is distributed to the commands of the Drina Corps, the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, communications regiment, the sector for morale, religious, and legal affairs, again, that's General Gvero; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And a bunch of other brigades. And we see the final line underlined "to the commander personally." I want to go through some of the elements of this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object. This has nothing to do with Tolimir. The document isn't even registered as such. I don't know what the foundation is for the -- for the assertion that I know about this document because it wasn't even sent to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, especially as you are using this document in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The issue of authenticating P125, as we have seen, can be approached from a number of angles, establishing whether it reflects accurately the events on the ground, as we did with the intercepts and Mr. Blaszczyk's testimony about what he learned from various witnesses himself pertaining to the situation on the ground that was reflected in that document. What this document is being used to show is that, in fact, those proposed measures in P125 were acted upon by General Mladic, having received that proposal. He was one of the recipients in the proposal's "to" list as we saw a moment ago, as was General Gvero. And one of the ways that we can further authenticate P125 is by showing that in fact it was received and acted upon, and General Mladic issued an order based on it, reflecting some of those proposals. And I intend to go through the document and examine the elements which flow from P125.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you restrict your questioning to those portion and for that purpose, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at paragraph 1, please, point 1 of this order, it says: "... prevent the entry of all uninvited individuals to the area of combat operations in the general sector of Srebrenica and Zepa." And, sir, how does that correspond, based on your work, your investigation, your familiarity with P125, with any of the proposed measures in P125, the Borike proposed order -- proposals and order?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is continuation of the proposal from this Borike document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we can, can we put in the English -- actually, let me consult with the expert here, with the Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we can, what I'd like to do is put the English translation of P125 next to the English translation of 65 ter 2100. And then -- and I will read the appropriate portions which then can get translated into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And after that both documents could be shown on the screen side by side in B/C/S. After that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: After that, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So you just told us that it corresponds to P125 and this prohibiting access to all unauthorised -- I'm sorry, the preventing entry of all uninvited individuals to the area of combat operations, what does that correspond to in P125, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It corresponds to the first point: "Prohibit access to all unauthorised individuals, filming and photographing of prisoners."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then we see in item 2, closing down -- I'm sorry, did you --

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, and item 2 is: "Until further notice, close the Konjevic Polje-Kravica-Bratunac and Rogatica-Borike-Visegrad roads to traffic, except for the vehicles of the VRS and MUP units engaged in combat operations." It corresponds to point 2 from the Borike order: "Prohibit traffic for all United Nations vehicles en route Zvornik-Vlasenica until further notice ..." And point 3 from the order of General Mladic: "Set up roadblocks and check-points for the regulation and control of traffic at the crossroads in Konjevic Polje and road leading out of Bratunac towards Kravica and the Rogatica-Borike and Visegrad-Borike roads." As we see here on the Borike order, Borike document, it does correspond to -- to the point, also 2, from Borike.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then again in item 4 of Mladic's order where he's preventing the entry of all local and foreign journalists, except for those approved by the VRS press centre, what proposal from the Borike proposal and order does that correspond to?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we see in the point 1 from this Borike document we see: "Prohibit access to all unauthorised individuals, filming and photographing of prisoners."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look at item 5 of General Mladic's order, where he again orders the banning and preventing of giving of information, issuing of announcements --

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- particularly in the issue of prisoners of war, evacuated civilians, and so forth. What proposed measure from the Borike proposal and order does that pertain to, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could be point 1 and point 3 from the Borike document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. President, I have couple more questions for Mr. Blaszczyk, but I see we're at the break and I can finish very quickly after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We must have the first break now and we will resume at 11.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before we continue with the document we were reviewing before the break, Mr. Blaszczyk, I just wanted to clarify one thing you said, and this was at page 24, line 22. I asked you the question: "Based on your investigation, what organs within the VRS were responsible for regulating traffic and setting up check-points?" And your answer was: "It was the military police of the VRS under the command of the security branch." We're going to hear, I'm sure, plenty of testimony from VRS officers from the time and probably some expert testimony as well on this issue, but I want to clarify one thing you said here. When you refer to "under the command of the security branch," I want to ask you whether that's in fact correct or whether there's a different relationship between the security branch and the military police that we sometimes refer to as professional control or guidance or management as opposed to "command" in the sense of a commander commanding the unit.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The microphone of the witness is not activated. Now everything is okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my experience during this investigation, which I took part in this investigation relating to the fall of Srebrenica, I met and interviewed many military police officers, VRS military police officers. And of course they were directed from both, let's say from Bratunac Brigade, from Zvornik Brigade, and they were of course directed to the commander of the brigades, but they were receiving orders from the security officer of the brigade. And I believe this is the -- and I'm sure that the security branch had kind of the control on the police, of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. As I said, we'll be hearing from other witnesses on this topic, so I'll just leave it there. Now, do we still have 65 ter 2100 on the screen? Okay. Sir, shortly before we took the recess, General Tolimir again suggested that P125, the document we see on the left, the Borike proposal -- proposals and order, was planted or is in some other way inauthentic. Now, having seen the original of General Mladic's order on the right, and I think we've all seen now the original version with Danko Gojkovic's inked signature, indicating that the Rogatica Brigade received that order at 2230 hours, how, if at all, did locating this document in the Drina Corps collection affect your conclusion as an investigator, in combination with the other elements of authentication that you've already talked about, that P125 is an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering this order and also intercept and witness statement and testimony, I can conclude only that this is authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We've heard a lot of references to the "Atlantida" binder, this collection of documents that you talked about, that you found bound together with this telegram, "Telegrami" heading and "Atlantida" written on it, as you've testified. It's been separated out now so that we can have each document in an individual folder. General Tolimir claimed that with the exception of what he said were the first three documents - and this is at transcript page 3682, line 3, yesterday - which were produced by logistics organs: "The rest contains telegrams which were written by me," General Tolimir, "and which you" - meaning you - "called "'Atlantida.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: First of all, just so that there's no doubt on the record -- and with the Usher's assistance, I just ask that the cover --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- be handed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, you will recall that I asked earlier to have the B/C/S versions of both documents side by side on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, you did, Mr. President. I apologise. If -- as soon as the hardest-working man in the courtroom gets back, if we could have that up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir and Mr. Gajic, you have now the B/C/S versions of both documents on the screen. I know you know the documents. It's not -- nothing new, but I think you should have the chance to have a look at this stage. Is that sufficient? Okay. Then please carry on, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now, if we may have P469 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that -- there we go. Sir, did you or anyone from OTP write "Telegrami 28/34" on this document?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. As I said, I think, yesterday, that no one from OTP made any redaction or correction in this -- our evidence in documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this word "Atlantida" here, did anybody from OTP write that?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you have or anybody from the OTP have anything to do with how these documents in this so-called "Atlantida" binder came to be placed within this "Atlantida" binder?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one from OTP. I believe no one from Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General Tolimir also suggested that the OTP was somehow selective in the documents that were in this binder and claimed that they all were written by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I would offer the entire "Atlantida" binder into evidence at this time. Each of the pages already has a P number because it was listed on one of the Defence cross-examination lists. We may have to postpone for a period of time the actual tendering process because it's a considerable number of numbers, but I can easily get that to Registry in time to take care of that as early as Monday. But I think it will become clear when one looks at the individual documents in the "Atlantida" binder that they emanate from a number of individuals and officers, not just General Tolimir. And I can take Mr. Blaszczyk through some of these documents now and just show them to the Trial Chamber, or I can just offer them to the Trial Chamber and at the Trial Chamber's leisure you can see for yourself that the signatories include other members of the Rogatica Brigade, General Krstic, for example, from the Drina Corps, and others. I'm happy to take some additional time and go through some of the individual documents if that's the Court's preference or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My objection is this: The "Atlantis" title is something I wanted to check. I wanted to check its authenticity. I asked the witness before, in my earlier cross-examination two months ago, he said that he had found such an original in the Drina Corps collection. But yesterday he said that this was given to him by Colonel Acimovic -- or some other colonel. And now I don't know -- I mean, we need to establish that something is authentic before it is admitted into evidence, and I think that should also apply to the "Atlantis" document. Danko Gojkovic said that that was the first time he was seeing the document and he said that when he was here to testify. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think we would like to hear something if you agree to tendering -- the tendering of the whole document by the Prosecution, or if you are in agreement with this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document has already been admitted. It was not admitted through this witness. The entire "Atlantis" binder. I thought at the time that it was an original until Danko said that he had never seen it before. So now there is the question of the authenticity of the actual cover itself, not of the documents that are in the binder. I am objecting to the admission of something that has not been verified and authenticated and we're not sure if that is an original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Blaszczyk has been crystal clear on a number of occasions with the Trial Chamber about the form in which he found the "Atlantida" binder, the circumstances under which he first saw it, and how it was processed, and how it came to be into the courtroom today. General Tolimir has directly challenged the authenticity of selected documents from the "Atlantida" binder. He has sought to admit certain of the documents when it suits him, but he is vigorously challenging the authenticity of other documents. And he is specifically in addition challenging how this "Atlantida" binder was put together. And we've already heard testimony from general -- from Mr. Blaszczyk about his efforts to interview an individual he thinks, based on his investigation, may have some knowledge about how this particular mini collection of documents within the Drina Corps collection was put together. On that note, we have filed a motion on the 18th of June, seeking to add that witness to the Prosecution's list of witnesses. We may need a Court order if the Court grants our motion to bring that witness here, but that will be for another day. In any event, General Tolimir has placed the authenticity of this group of documents directly at issue. Again, he has suggested that certain documents, including P125, was planted. I think it would be helpful for the Trial Chamber to see exactly how these documents lay together, as Mr. Blaszczyk has told the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we delete the untruths from the transcript. All I am disputing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, sorry -- no, we can't delete anything from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I did not dispute a series of documents. We have been working for two days now, and all I'm disputing is the title of this document, "Atlantida," because I'm saying that this part where it says "telegrams," the witness did not write that and that he did not write "Atlantida." And I disputed the document P125, which was on the screen a little bit earlier. I did not dispute any other document and it has been said -- stated here that Tolimir disputed a series of other documents which is not true. I put in an objection because the transcript is recording what appear to be untruths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, we can't delete anything from the transcript. What is said is said and it is recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. I misspoke. What I meant was to correct the errors, not to delete anything from the transcript. I wanted my truth to be recorded as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is recorded, and the Trial Chamber will consider the positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, Mr. Thayer, I think all parts of this binder are already in evidence as single and separate exhibits. What about this cover page, is that part of one of these exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We were just doing the same exercise, Mr. President, that is, 469. And we'll let the trial -- that also came in apparently through Mr. Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Gajic in agreement. And therefore, what is the purpose of your tendering the whole document as one new exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, if everything is in separately, then there is no need to re-admit, obviously, everything as one big exhibit. The idea is for they -- for the documents to be in a particular order in which they were found so the Trial Chamber can at least see that, so you can see how these documents lay inside this binder. So I understand that they came in in bits and pieces through Mr. Gojkovic, but the idea is to make them available to the Trial Chamber in a form where you can see how this binder existed when Mr. Blaszczyk first laid his hands and eyes on it. Perhaps we can put our thinking hats on over the weekend and figure out some way of doing that without giving everything a new number and we can come back to the Trial Chamber easily on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber appreciates this proposal because otherwise we are really confused at the end. But you could show this binder as you have it with you in the original form to the witness, to the Chamber, and to the Defence, and we can, without going through all documents, I think this is not the purpose of re-examination, let's have a look -- let the witness have a look on it, if he can say anything about his recognition. Mr. Blaszczyk, could you say something, do you recognise anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As I said some time ago, I recognise this binder. The cover page is very clear for me, that at first time I seen this cover page, the entire small binder called "Atlantida" in Zagreb, at the field office in Zagreb. And the collection of the documents seized by ICTY from MUP, RS MUP, and RS MOD arrived to Zagreb on the 17th December 2004. During the next -- the following two days and on the 17th as well, I reviewed almost entire -- almost entire collection and I remember this binder very clear. The documents from this collection I am keeping in my hands right now, they were clipped together. And the first page we see on the screen, it was the first, the cover page, of this binder in the same shape, except of course ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please have a look at the first page where you find "Atlantida" in front of you. In the original, not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can confirm, it's the same shape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I thought since the witness said that the first time he saw the document was in Zagreb and that they were seized from the Ministry of Defence and from the MUP, but these documents were in the OTP office in Banja Luka, then the question could be the order in which they were arranged because the witness is claiming something else than what another witness said, that the binder was arranged in a different way. Perhaps this is something that could be clarified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, first I think it would be helpful to have a direct citation of who this alleged witness is and what he said and when he allegedly said it about this binder, if General Tolimir's serious about what he just said. Otherwise, I'm not sure it's helpful to go any further. Mr. Blaszczyk has made it clear, once again, the circumstances under which he first laid his eyes and hands on the "Atlantida" binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you have any further questions for Mr. Blaszczyk --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, I do not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- in relation to "Atlantida"?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No questions further at all, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then the binder should be shown to the Chamber and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, just one additional question while you're looking at the originals there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think we went into this many moons ago when you first testified, but how were these -- you said they were clipped together. How were these actually clipped together, this collection of "Atlantida" documents?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clipped together in the same order we see these documents right now. The procedure here is that when the binder or whatever document arrive into The Hague, it's accepted by Evidence Unit, even if this is a binder, the documents are clipped together, the documents are separated from the binder and are stamped in the same order by people from Evidence Unit, giving to the particular page, the following pages, the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And I really want to get down to basics. When you found this "Atlantida" binder, physically what was binding those pages together? What was the actual binder? Was it a black, plastic clip? Was it something with forks? What was holding it together?
