utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We see on this cover page and on the pages following two holes. It was clipped by a metal - I don't know how to call in English - piece of metal together and clipped together.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And so who stuck the individual pages that we -- that the Trial Chamber has before it in those blue folders?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the people from Evidence Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaszczyk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have a question, more a clarification from the witness. We have heard a lot of evidence regarding authentication of documents. Can I ask you as a professional policeman to explain the following: Authentication of document, is it a special skill that can be possessed by a policeman in any police force or is it the specialised training?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course the authentication of documents can be done by the experts and in some extent by the police officers also because they are working with these type of cases. And they have also kind of expertised knowledge about how to deal with these type of documents. But in this case, if you are talking about this particular case, it is a little bit difficult because it is not typical police case because we have received the documents after so many years, when the documents were produced and kept in, let's say, not so good condition even for the documents, and so many people touched these documents, we couldn't make any, let's say, additional expertise regarding the authenticity of the documents. General Tolimir mentioned some time ago about finger-prints and other -- this type of stuff. We are limited to other, let's say, option of the investigation how to authenticate this document, this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just a follow-up question to that one. Can any policeman authenticate a document and give a conclusive opinion that is original or not original?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so that this is possible for any policeman. Policeman should have a knowledge about that list, about these type of the documents, you should have experience about these type of the documents, you should have knowledge about the case, and should be involved in the investigation. I don't think that a policeman, for example, from the patrol policeman or policeman from other unit, could authenticate these documents having these documents in his hands right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I now turn to the binder, the "Atlantida" binder, the folders of which I have here. And I'm trying to understand what you meant by "they were clipped."

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- you will see on this, each page of this -- each document from this binder you see two holes over there, starting from -- yes, starting from cover page, "Atlantida" page, and the following pages, they have the holes also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, maybe -- I'm not following you. I haven't seen the page that is written "Atlantida." So if you give me a moment, I will find it.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this is the cover page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: This is the cover page?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, this is the cover page. Yes, I'm referring to cover page, it is in Cyrillic "Atlantida" written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Okay. Sorry. All these individual pieces of paper in one of these folders together form what we are referring to as the "Atlantida" binder; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, Mr. Tolimir, do you want to see this collection as well? It should be transferred. Mr. Blaszczyk, I have an additional question and I would like to take you back, and this has something to do with this binder as well, to your evidence of yesterday at page 31, lines 14 through 19 of the transcript of yesterday. You said, and I quote: "I can exclude that this document was added to this collection in Zagreb, Banja Luka, since the entire collection was in the possession of the ICTY. I can exclude this possibility 100 per cent sure. Everything is possible that it was added sometime later, but I don't think so why it should be done in this way. But physically it is possible because we had no control of this documentation at that time." I have -- I found the impression that there is a certain contradiction. Could you explain your answer of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour. I made mistake here, of course. Before we received this collection, it was possible that somebody could put whatever binder or any document in this collection because we had no control on this collection; but since we got this collection in Zagreb and later on in The Hague, nobody could add or redact anything from this collection. I am 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means the relevant sentence should read as follows: Everything is possible that we -- that it was added sometime earlier.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Blaszczyk, I think you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- and the questioning put to you. Thank you very much for your attendance here in this courtroom again, and you are free now to return to your normal professional activities. Thank you very much again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now you may leave the courtroom because we have to deal with some matters with documents, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, my first question is: Did you notify the Defence about the documents you were using during re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did not notify the Defence about my re-examination documents. It's something that I had to put together very quickly, as you may recall, yesterday during breaks and, frankly, I was still preparing late into the night last night. So I simply did not have an opportunity to put any list together. If -- my practice is certainly if there's something that's never been seen before or something that's going to come out of the blue, I will make particular effort to get that to the Defence ahead of time so they know it's coming, and we'll continue to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... follow your position. Especially with this witness and this re-examination, you had the opportunity after preparing the continuation of the re-examination, even it was perhaps last night, late in the night. It should have been possible to notify the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If the Court wishes that to be our practice, we will adopt that practice forthwith, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was already the practice as you did it with the witness Ruez. I think there was several instances you did that if you wanted to -- especially if you wanted to use new documents to challenge the cross-examination. The Chamber would appreciate that. Now I would like to come back to the list of different documents we haven't received yet. There were so many we have marked for identification, and if I look at the transcript of the 27th of April this year, the -- when the witness was the first time here in the trial, we had some problems with your motion to -- and your tendering the documents. Therefore, we have a long list of documents marked for identification and you are still tendering them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That is P121 up through P154. And I believe that P120, which was the map marked by Mr. Blaszczyk, has already been tendered. So the rest are 121 through 154, and I don't think there are any gaps in that series of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They all will be received with the given numbers by the Registry, and I think they all have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, as for the documents used in redirect, 410 and 411 are already in evidence. 765, which is the third intercept from the 21st Division notebook, was technically recently admitted via the Trial Chamber's decision on the 92 bis motion because this intercept operator who took that intercept was one of the proposed 92 bis witnesses. So I think it's probably just better to sit on that and wait until that comes in through the 92 bis process of uploading and everything. That was Witness number 106.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which document are you referring to at the moment? Can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That was 65 ter number 765, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. We leave it for a later stage. And what about the 65 ter 2100 you used today?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, we would tender that, Mr. President, at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P655.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I was told that the document just received, P145 through P152, have no translation. Do you intend to provide the Chamber with a translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We'll take a look, see if we've got one that hasn't surfaced for some reason, and if not, we'll submit it and get those to the Trial Chamber and Registry a.s.a.p.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The documents P145, P147, P148, P149, P151, and P5 -- P152 will be marked for identification pending translation. Are there other matters related to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Not to this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then I have to deal with some other matters related to exhibits. P15 and P16, both intercepts, have some irregularities of the exhibit numbers. They are numbered with P15.1 through P15.5 and P16.1 through P16.5. The translations are not attached to the documents but have a separate number, P15.2. Since these are intercepts and the Registry has numbered all intercepts with A and B, for instance, P15A instead of P15.1, the Chamber asks the Prosecution to identify the correct translation for each document. The Registry would then renumber them; mark them as exhibit if they have a translation; mark them as MFI if they don't; and then file a memo on the record explaining that. That was the first matter. The second is related to P162D, also intercept document. It was MFI'd. This intercept exhibit was admitted without translation. There is now a translation available and this -- its MFI status can be changed to an exhibit. The third matter is related to documents tendered by the accused, D2, D21, and D31. They are all MFI'd pending translation. We have received now translations, thus they can be admitted as exhibits. I see Mr. Gajic is in agreement with that. And the last matter is Exhibit D15, it was given a wrong 65 ter number. Would you, Mr. Gajic, correct that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honours. The correct 65 ter number of this document is 1D58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's another document, P162C, that has no translation and it will be -- only be marked for identification pending translation. I hope we have now solved all problems with exhibit numbers. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just three administrative or housekeeping matters, Mr. President. The first is I just wanted to note while we're on -- fresh on the topic, we do have this motion to add a witness to the 65 ter list. And I won't -- it's a confidential motion so I won't say anything further, but again we may need to apply to the Trial Chamber should the Chamber grant the motion for a production order to get this reluctant individual here. So I just want to put that on the horizon for sometime after the recess. The second item is we understand the issue with, for example, P15 and 16 that Your Honour spoke about at the beginning. That's obviously a vestige of the old numbering system, and particularly as it relates to the 92 bis decision, we're going to need to convert all those, run them through the new machine, and pop out the new numbers. That is going to take some time and effort for the team to go through each of those packages and do that. I note that in the Trial Chamber's decision there's a 30-day dead-line for a number of actions that we are required to take. Given that we're on the cusp of the summer recess and particularly given the amount of work that's going to be required for each of those witnesses, to identify every exhibit that was not only admitted through the witness but shown to the witness; not admitted through the witness, shown to the witness; admitted through another witness, all our fun categories, that's going to take a significant amount of time, certainly more than 30 days, particularly with the summer recess upon us. So we would ask for at least another 30 days to complete that project because it is a substantial project to have to go through each of those witnesses. It requires going through all their testimony page by page to make sure we're not missing any exhibits. Basically it means compiling all those witness exhibit lists now, so -- and that is -- it is a tremendous time investment for us per witness. So we would ask for at least another 30 days to complete that project.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, do you want to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no comments about these things. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, we will consider your motion and come back to that on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Lastly, I just wanted to alert the Trial Chamber to one exhibit-related issue for the upcoming witness on Monday, General Nicolai. He will follow an intercept operator who I think will be somewhat brief, but we will hear from General Nicolai starting on Monday, and I think we're all in agreement that General Nicolai will be on the stand for some time. We've already arranged for him to come back and be available the first day we're all back in court after the recess. The Court may be aware that there have been recent searches conducted by the Serbian authorities of residences and other locations related to its ongoing search for Ratko Mladic. That material has been disclosed to us from the Serbian authorities. We are in the process of processing all of it and trying to get it in a disclosable form to the Defence. Part of that material, we have learned, are cassette recordings that apparently were done by either General Mladic or somebody close to him of conversations involving various Main Staff officers and in some cases UNPROFOR officers, including General Nicolai. What we have tried to do is expedite the transcription of those cassette recordings -- actually, we've tried to expedite first the digitisation of those cassette recordings so that we can put them in a format that can be disclosed to the Defence and we've tried very hard to get that done as soon as possible, particularly given General Nicolai's upcoming testimony. Some of these conversations are between General Nicolai and General Tolimir. So we have expedited the transcription process, literally writing out transcripts from those cassettes. We've just disclosed the B/C/S version because we start off with the original language to the accused. We finally got those done yesterday, they've gone over. I should have the English translations of those by the end of today, and as soon as I get them they'll go over. I've not seen them. I don't know what they look like. There are five of them. I think they're very short. But the most important thing is that, from what we can tell, is they relate -- they're the same conversations as were intercepted by some of the intercept operators you've heard from which are already part of General Nicolai's exhibit list. So what we have on General Nicolai's exhibit list are various intercepts in which he was a participant. We have the UN notes of those conversations. You've seen some examples of those through Colonel Fortin when he was taking notes. Now what we have appears to be General Mladic of the Main Staff's own recordings of those conversations so we can hear in some cases a side of the conversation that we couldn't hear in the intercept. You may recall General Tolimir referring to some monologues where you only heard one side of the conversation. Now we've got cassettes that we believe will dovetail with some of the intercepts that are already on General Nicolai's list. All of that to say the new cassette material doesn't have a 65 ter number, so it's not on our 65 ter list. But what we propose to do, which is what we've done in other cases where we have audio-tapes of conversations, is simply make that part of the consolidated intercept exhibit. By that I mean we have the notebook if there was a notebook, print-out, audio-tape, and then transcript of the audio-tape. The system we're using now is that all four of those related exhibits come under one 65 ter number. So what we propose to do is when we get these documents in an uploadable form is to enter those under the existing 65 ter number for that intercept. So I just wanted to alert the Trial Chamber to that ahead of time, and I'll liaise with the Defence on that over the weekend before General Nicolai testifies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this information. This is very helpful and, indeed, you should contact the Defence and liaise with the Defence on the best way to -- of disclosure and to deal with these different documents and cassettes. Are there any other housekeeping matters for today? This is not the case, then we adjourn and resume on Monday, in the afternoon, 2.15, in Courtroom I. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
